blocks.text: A similar Mishnaic report is referred to the same scene (Derenbourg, Essai [=Derenbourg, Essai sur l'histoire et la géographie de la Palestine] 98; Schürer^{2} [=Schürer, Geschichte des jüdischen Volkes, 2nd ed.] 1, 224; Grätz, hebr. [=Graetz, Geschichte, Hebrew transl. by Rabinowitz] 1, 448). Some centuries later the scene repeats itself: the inhabitants of Maḥuza pelt R. [=Rabbi] Zeïra, who makes a remark displeasing to them, with their citrons (Kidd. [=Kiddushin] 73^{a}; Derenbourg a. O. [=at the place cited]).

The identification of the fruit of the goodly tree with the eṯrōg is an undisputed tradition within rabbinic Judaism (Maim. [=Maimonides], Introduction to the Mischnakomment. [=Mishnah commentary] f. [=folio] 54^{a} Romm [=Romm edition (Vilna)]; Maim. H. Lulab [=Hilkhot Lulav, Maimonides, Mishneh Torah] 7, 2; L. Löw gS. [=Leopold Löw, Gesammelte Schriften] 1, 280). The necessity of a Sinaitic tradition is proven precisely by the fact that the identification of the eṯrōg with the fruit required in the Bible cannot otherwise be justified (Leon da Modena, Bechinaṯ hadaṯ [=Leon da Modena, Beḥinat ha-Dat] 26). This is still emphasized — in accordance with the traditional view — by Chajim Sofer, rabbi of the orth. [=Orthodox] congregation in Budapest (Kōl Sofer [=Chajim Sofer, Kol Sofer], 1882, note on Abot [=Pirqe Abot] 3, 1). Maimūnī [=Maimonides] attempted a rational justification: the eṯrōg is suitable because it stays fresh throughout the entire duration of the festival, which cannot be said of peaches, pomegranates, quinces or pears (More [=Moreh Nevukhim] 3, 43 end). In point of fact this hardly holds true for pomegranates and quinces.

In Talmudic times the philological conscience sought aggadic supports for the equation hādār = eṯrōg; later, etymological justifications were sought for it. Nachmānī [=Nachmanides, Commentary on the Pentateuch] (Emor [=Parashat Emor] 106^{a}; Meiri, Magen Abot [=Menahem ha-Meiri, Magen Avot] 111 Last; Rapoport, Erech Millin [=Rapoport, Erekh Millin] 253) ingeniously, but incorrectly, tries to extract from eṯrōg a root רגג, which is supposed to correspond to the hebr. [=Hebrew] הדר. For him the eṯrōg is the fruit of Paradise that arouses desire — רגג. It led Eve into sin; therefore, together with other plants, it is to serve for atonement. As late as 1819 M. J. Landau [=Moses Israel Landau, ed. of the Aruch] (Ar. [=Aruch, ed. Landau] 1, 231) attempts to derive etymologically “to gild,” thus golden fruit, and Kohut [=Aruch, ed. Kohut] asserts (1, 336; 8, 274) that p. [=Persian] ترنك [turunk] is synonymous with hādār (?) and wishes to find in this the justification of the traditional identification.
In the 13th century Eleazar of Worms calculated that the numerical value of פרי עץ הדר, 659, is the same as that of the word [א]תרוגים (Rokeach [=Sefer ha-Roqeaḥ by Eleazar of Worms] 39^{b} Zolkiew).
